passage: Alka had come to Ujjain only for a conference, but her colleague Dilnaz insisted they see the temple on festival night. At eleven the rain started, hard and sudden, and the whole queue surged toward the one covered corridor. Alka felt the push at her back and grabbed the railing. Most people just pulled dupattas over their heads and shuffled on, patient, some even laughing. A handful of young men shoved forward, shouting, and an old woman ahead lost her footing. Dilnaz caught her elbow. Alka remembered the green exit sign she had noticed near the shoe stand. "Left," she said. "The side gate." The three of them edged out of the press, the old woman between them, into a lane where a tea seller had a tarpaulin up. The old woman laughed, soaked, and blessed them both.

qa.q: Where had Alka noticed the green exit sign?
qa.a: She had noticed it near the shoe stand.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling when she felt the push at her back?
qa.a: Alka was alarmed and tense, grabbing the railing, but stayed clear-headed enough to remember the exit.

qa.q: Which habits helped Alka and Dilnaz get out safely?
qa.a: Noticing the exit beforehand, staying calm in the surge, and helping the unsteady old woman instead of pushing.

qa.q: How might the old woman have experienced the rush?
qa.a: She was probably frightened when she lost her footing and then grateful and relieved, which is why she laughed and blessed them.

grounding: It illustrates a visitor who sees a festival crowd surge in the rain, notices most people stay patient while a few shove, and relies on calm, knowing the exit and helping the vulnerable.

passage: In a back garden in Leeds, Aiko kicked the football too hard and it smashed Mr. Patel's kitchen window next door. Aiko ran inside and hid under the stairs, heart hammering. When Mr. Patel knocked, Aiko's mum came to find her. "Was it you?" "No. Amara was kicking it," Aiko said, and felt sick saying it. Amara, from two doors down, hadn't even been out that afternoon. That night Aiko couldn't eat her rice. At last Aiko whispered the truth. Mum didn't shout. "Thank you for telling me. Now we tell Mr. Patel, and Amara." Next morning they stood on his step together. Aiko's voice wobbled. "I broke it. And I said it was Amara. I'm sorry." Mr. Patel nodded slowly. "That took courage. You can help me sweep up the glass."

qa.q: Whose window did the football smash?
qa.a: It smashed Mr. Patel's kitchen window.

qa.q: How did Aiko feel after blaming Amara?
qa.a: Aiko felt sick and guilty, unable even to eat her rice that night.

qa.q: Why was facing Mr. Patel with Mum better than hiding?
qa.a: Owning up in person, with a parent beside her, let Aiko take responsibility, clear Amara's name and help repair things by sweeping the glass.

qa.q: How might Amara have felt if the blame had stuck?
qa.a: Amara would likely have felt confused and hurt, blamed for something while not even outside that afternoon.

grounding: It illustrates a child who breaks a neighbour's window, hides and blames another child, then faces the neighbour with a parent and says sorry.

passage: Okay, so here's the cricket war of Block D. I'm Jeevan, sixteen, and every evening we play in the lane behind our building. Last month Rashmi Aunty from the ground floor came out shouting that the ball hits her window and the noise wakes her mother. She complained to the society secretary, and we got a letter. I was so angry. Other kids play too, but the letter had my name on it. It felt like she'd picked me. My dad said, "Go and talk to her, not about her." So I did. Turns out her mother is ninety and sleeps from two till five. And the ball really had cracked a pane once. We made a deal: we play after five, tennis ball only, and nobody bowls from her end. Last Sunday she even came out to watch a super over.

qa.q: When does Rashmi Aunty's mother sleep?
qa.a: She sleeps from two till five.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan feel angry about the letter?
qa.a: Jeevan felt singled out and unfairly targeted, since other kids play too but only Jeevan's name was on it.

qa.q: What made the compromise work?
qa.a: Jeevan talked to Rashmi Aunty directly, heard her reasons, and they agreed on a time, a softer ball and a different bowling end.

qa.q: How might Rashmi Aunty have seen the evening cricket?
qa.a: She was probably worried and tired, protecting her ninety-year-old mother's sleep and a window that had already cracked once.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who feels targeted by a neighbour's noise complaint, and a polite compromise on time and volume that ends the dispute.

passage: Vaibhav had seven minutes to reach his placement interview when he found Sangeeta's scooter parked squarely in front of his bike in the building's cramped stilt parking. Again. He leaned on her doorbell. "Move it. You do this every day." Sangeeta came out in her office clothes, keys in hand, just as late. "You park across two spots every night. I have no choice." His voice rose. Giving in felt like losing. Then the lift opened and the society secretary, Mr. Rao, stepped out holding his tiffin. He looked at both of them and at his watch. "Both of you, go. Tonight, eight o'clock, bring the parking map." That night the map showed a numbered spot for each flat that nobody had ever painted. Vaibhav and Sangeeta painted them together the next Sunday, arguing only about the colour.

qa.q: How many minutes did Vaibhav have to reach his interview?
qa.a: He had seven minutes.

qa.q: Why did giving in feel like losing to Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt frustrated and proud, worried that moving first would make him look weak.

qa.q: What settled the fight without lasting bitterness?
qa.a: Using the society's parking map at a calm meeting, which showed numbered spots, and then painting them together.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta see the parking problem?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt she had no choice because Vaibhav parked across two spots every night, so she was just as frustrated and late.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who argues over parking and feels that giving in means weakness, until calm talk and the housing society's rules settle it.

passage:
First Sunday. Karthik went to his first residents' association meeting because the lift had been broken for three weeks. Two retired men did all the talking; everyone else stared at their phones. When Yamini from 3B tried to speak about the lift, the treasurer said, "Next agenda," and she sat down.
Second Sunday. Karthik came early, with Yamini and three others from the upper floors. He had printed the association's own by-laws. "Sir, clause 6 says any member can add an agenda item in writing. Here is ours: the lift, with quotes from two repair firms." The room went quiet. The treasurer frowned, then read the paper.
Fourth Sunday. The lift was working. At the meeting, Karthik noticed three people who had never spoken before raise their hands. The chairman now kept a list of speakers on the whiteboard.

qa.q: Which clause did Karthik point to?
qa.a: Clause 6, which says any member can add an agenda item in writing.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt at the first meeting when Yamini was cut off?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt frustrated and uneasy at how two men dominated and a neighbour was silenced.

qa.q: Which of Karthik's steps changed how the meetings worked?
qa.a: Showing up with neighbours, bringing the written by-laws, and adding a clear agenda item with repair quotes.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt at the second meeting?
qa.a: Yamini probably felt supported and less alone, since her lift concern was finally heard with others backing her.

grounding: It illustrates a young resident who notices a few people dominating a housing society meeting and helps it work for all by showing up, using written rules and speaking fairly.

passage:
Monday. Harsha came home at eleven after her hospital shift and heard it through the stairwell window: "Every night so late. And that boy on the bike dropping her. God knows what her parents think." It was Lakshmi Aunty from the first floor. Harsha's face burned. She wanted to bang on the door.
Wednesday. Harsha met Lakshmi Aunty at the milk booth. Instead of looking away, she smiled. "Aunty, I'm on night duty in the emergency ward this month. Arjun, the boy on the bike, is my colleague; he lives nearby." Lakshmi Aunty blinked. "Oh. Emergency? That must be tiring."
Saturday. Lakshmi Aunty knocked with a steel box of lemon rice. "For after your duty." Harsha noticed the whispers on the stairs had gone quiet. She never did find out whether Aunty had changed her mind, or just her topic.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi Aunty bring on Saturday?
qa.a: She brought a steel box of lemon rice.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel on Monday when she heard the gossip?
qa.a: Harsha felt angry and humiliated, her face burning with an urge to bang on the door.

qa.q: Why did Harsha's approach at the milk booth work?
qa.a: She stayed polite and open, simply sharing the facts about her shift and her colleague, which left the gossip nothing to feed on.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Aunty have seen Harsha after the milk booth?
qa.a: Lakshmi Aunty seemed surprised and a little sheepish, then concerned, even bringing lemon rice for after Harsha's duty.

grounding: It illustrates a young person gossiped about by neighbours who responds with a steady, polite and open manner that starves the gossip.

passage:
Diwali week. Irawati, new to the building, carried a plate of kaju katli to every flat on her floor, including the Deshmukhs, who had never once nodded back in the lift. Jahnavi Deshmukh took the plate at the door without a smile.
A Tuesday in January. At midnight the Deshmukhs' door banged open: Jahnavi's father had collapsed in the bathroom. Irawati, still awake, ran over, called the ambulance and held the lift while the paramedics came up. She sat with Jahnavi in the hospital corridor till four.
March. A leak from Irawati's flat stained the Deshmukhs' ceiling. Irawati braced for a fight when Jahnavi rang the bell. Instead Jahnavi said, "The plumber can come Thursday. Split the bill?" They settled it in five minutes, over tea, and Jahnavi returned the Diwali plate she had kept since October.

qa.q: What sweet did Irawati carry to every flat?
qa.a: She carried a plate of kaju katli.

qa.q: What did Irawati feel when Jahnavi rang the bell in March?
qa.a: Irawati felt anxious, bracing for a fight over the leak.

qa.q: Why was the March problem so easy to solve?
qa.a: The goodwill Irawati had built, from Diwali sweets to sitting with Jahnavi at the hospital, made Jahnavi ready to cooperate rather than fight.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt sitting with Irawati in the hospital corridor?
qa.a: Jahnavi was likely frightened for her father and deeply grateful not to be alone, which changed how she saw her neighbour.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who shares festival sweets and helps in an emergency, building goodwill that makes a later conflict easy to resolve.

passage: I'm Gopika, and I was buying bread when it started at the corner of our lane. Kiran's cart had knocked Salim bhai's scooter mirror. Just a mirror. Salim bhai shouted, Kiran shouted back, normal. Then a man I didn't know said, "These people always do this," and within a minute there were two groups, and the words were not about the mirror any more. I felt my own mouth open to say something about "those people", and I shut it. I stood between the groups and said loudly, "It's a mirror. Why are we talking about anyone's religion?" My voice shook. Somebody laughed nervously. Then I sent Kiran's neighbour to fetch Father Thomas from the school and Ustad Rafiq from the tea shop, two people everyone listens to. Within half an hour Kiran was paying for a new mirror, and Salim bhai was helping push the cart.

qa.q: What did Kiran's cart knock?
qa.a: It knocked Salim bhai's scooter mirror.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling while standing between the groups?
qa.a: Gopika was nervous, voice shaking, and had even felt a flash of the same anger before choosing not to join the labelling.

qa.q: Which steps stopped the quarrel spreading?
qa.a: Refusing to use group labels, bringing the talk back to the mirror, and fetching two elders everyone trusts.

qa.q: How might Salim bhai have felt once the elders arrived?
qa.a: Salim bhai probably felt calmer and less cornered, able to treat it as just a mirror again, which is why he helped push the cart.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees a small quarrel take on religious colour and stops it spreading by refusing labels, cooling the talk and fetching neutral elders.

passage: In Singapore, Chen posted a photo of the drawing he had spent all weekend on, a heron over the canal, and then refreshed the app every two minutes through dinner. Eleven likes. Then nothing for an hour. His chest felt heavy. At nine he deleted the post. His uncle Diego, visiting from Manila, found him on the balcony. "Where's the heron? I wanted to show your aunt." "I took it down. Nobody liked it." Diego raised an eyebrow. "Eleven people liked it. And so did I, and I don't even have an account." Chen almost laughed. "It's not the same." "I know. But the drawing didn't get worse between eight and nine. Only the number changed." Chen took out his sketchbook and looked at the heron again. It was still good.

qa.q: How many likes did Chen's post get?
qa.a: It got eleven likes.

qa.q: What was Chen feeling when he deleted the post?
qa.a: Chen felt low and disappointed, his chest heavy, as if the silence meant the drawing had no worth.

qa.q: How did Diego help Chen see the likes differently?
qa.a: Diego gently pointed out that the drawing didn't change, only the number did, separating Chen's work and worth from strangers' clicks.

qa.q: How might Diego see Chen's heron drawing?
qa.a: Diego clearly admires it, wanting to show it to Chen's aunt, and liked it without needing any app at all.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager whose mood rises and falls with likes, and an adult who gently shows that numbers do not measure a person or their work.

passage: In their Ghaziabad housing society, everyone in Class 9 was doing the same dance trend that week, and the version getting the most views was filmed on a terrace parapet with the city behind. Jyoti had the song stuck in her head all day. At four she messaged Chandrika: "Terrace at 5? Parapet version?" Chandrika replied, "No thanks. I'll film you on the ground though." Jyoti felt a sting. Was Chandrika calling her silly? On the terrace the wind pulled at her dupatta, and the drop looked much deeper than on screen. Chandrika stood by the stairs, phone ready, not arguing, just waiting. Jyoti stepped back. "Courtyard?" "Courtyard," Chandrika grinned. They did it eleven times, until they kept laughing mid-spin. The courtyard version got fewer views. Jyoti watched it twice before bed anyway.

qa.q: Where was the most-viewed version of the dance filmed?
qa.a: It was filmed on a terrace parapet with the city behind.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel when Chandrika said "No thanks"?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a sting of hurt, wondering if Chandrika thought the idea was silly.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's response show about fitting in?
qa.a: By refusing only the risky part, offering to film on the ground and staying friendly, Chandrika showed Jyoti could join the trend without the danger.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt standing by the stairs?
qa.a: Chandrika was probably worried about the drop but chose to wait calmly rather than argue, trusting Jyoti to decide.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager drawn to a risky version of a viral dance to fit in, and a friend who says no thanks, stays friends and shows another way to belong.
